[h1] A test of patience, perseverance, and determination [/h1]

Difficult, painstakingly tedious, and at times downright infuriating, Chip's Challenge lures unsuspecting players in with easy to grasp mechanics, simple enemies and items, and charming retro visuals. That being said, only the most masochistic of players will manage to stick around for the especially evil later levels: dying at a later part of the level and having to redo everything over and over again will be something you'll need to get used to. 

I want to highlight especially levels 133 Blobdance, 89 Block Buster, and 87 Cityblock, in descending 'suffering experienced' order. At least half of my playtime was concentrated in just these 3 levels - whereas other levels can be completed in a matter of minutes. Blobdance and Cityblock tried my patience like nothing else, though I would discover Block Buster to be significantly easier with pause buffering. 

Despite how (131) Totally Unfair some of the levels may be, Chip's Challenge still offers swaths of genuinely engaging and fun puzzles within its 150 levels. Take, say, 122 Totally Fair. You're tasked with acquiring 5 chips to get to the ending, 3 of which are right in front of your spawnpoint. However, trying to get the last two results in you getting stuck in a trap, and unable to move further. You'll have to brave venturing into the monster's territory to first survive, and then find a way to manipulate the chomper into [spoiler] standing on the unlock switch for you. [/spoiler] Solving that would draw out a sense of satisfaction out of anybody. But even better, is when you get to revisit the concept again in 131 Totally Unfair, and then you notice all the extra things put in place for you to redo the solution in an even more clever manner.

Similarly, many of the later levels, like 120 Alphabet Soup, 134 Pain, and 123 The Prisoner had me pleasantly surprised with their fair levels of difficulty, despite seeming virtually unapproachable at first. Being able to work through these puzzles from my childhood on the steam port of this game was a ton of fun, and well worth experiencing for honing one's puzzle-solving skills. 

PS. Hint for the final level: Block flicking is doable on the steam version, whereas it wasn't present in the original MS version. Block flicking is where you walk straight along besides a block, and just before you leave the tile, press the directional key as if you were to move into the block whilst still holding down the key to go straight. This makes this level so much more reasonable not having to die each time you check a block.

Like many, I was brought in by the nostalgia of days past.  However, I soon discovered why this game is even more notorious than I remembered.  

Summary: This is a punishing, but creative puzzle game that can send ten minutes (not exaggerating) of perfect progress out the window because of one incorrect keystroke.  There is no undo.  Do not try it.  If you want to get every achievement, definitely do not try it.

The good:
There are about 150 puzzles.  They are varied and inventive.  It's possible to reason your way through many of the puzzles and solve them.  
I'm told there's a lot of mods out there to give you more levels.  

The bad:
It's very easy to make mistakes on some of the harder puzzles.  Once you do that, it doesn't matter how well you were doing up to that point.  Start the level over.  
It took me about 48 hours to finish 149 levels.  I'm done, and I'm not touching this game again.

Bad:
There are levels where there is really no way to know the right option except by trial and error.  There are levels I had to consult guides rather than go through ten minutes of perfect steps only to find the block I moved had fire underneath it.  You know what?  I'd be able to tell if a block had fire under it BECAUSE IT WOULD BE HOT.  Then I would choose to NOT MOVE IT.  Oh, I can't swim?  I should be able to scramble back on shore.  Oh, and I can only swim with certain shoes.  Because reasons.  

The levels, while creative, can also get very, very repetitive.  That's tiring and dull.  But then you make a mistake and you have to do it again because your eyes glazed over.  

Would be nice to improve game:
-Something to slow the game down.  I'm looking at you, Block Buster.  Those blocks were moving so fast, they blur. 
-Saves/Checkpoints in levels.  Really, do we need to redo 10 minutes of block moving because the cat jumped on the keyboard?  
-Ability to pull or undo.  
-MOVE THE PAUSE BUTTON AWAY FROM THE NEXT/PREVIOUS LEVEL BUTTONS.  For goodness sake, why would you do that?  There's no prompt to say "You're in the middle of a level, do you want to change?"  It just changes the level.  If you meant to hit pause, too bad.  All the progress is lost.  

Summary:
Don't pick this up.  Don't pick it up on sale.  Save your time and play a game that respects you and your time.  This is a creative game, but . . . I wouldn't even recommend it on a budget.  It's just punishing and seems to enjoy making the player suffer.  That's not good gameplay.

[h1]Chip's Challenge to try & determine what the word 'puzzle' actually means.[/h1]

[b][u]PROS[/u]:[/b] Chip's Challenge is a tile based puzzle game, & is one of the more famous ones due to the implementation of power ups, unique enemy designs, & multiple early releases during the 90's.  The game does come with both visual styles, so those who were fans of the smoother design or the tile hopping Windows design have the option.  A good deal of the puzzles, especially in the first half, are quite well designed & feel rewarding to figure out the solution.  Even better, the game is free, letting anyone curious on the game's quality an easy check.

[b][u]CONS[/u]:[/b] A minor one to get out of the way first is the looping background music, which can get tedious after so much time playing it.  The real problem this game has is the difficulty come the latter half of the game.  Several levels are simply trials in frustration due to the sporadic enemy AI.  Multiple stages aren't even puzzles, just trial & error.  This is made worse from any death or mess up meaning having to replay the stage all over again.  Play a stage for 10 minutes & push one block one space too far?  Start the entire thing over again.  A stage is not a puzzle if they require a stage played perfectly until the 8 minute mark, then provide the player with two blocks, one with the goal & one with an instant kill fire under it that one wouldn't know about unless they had a map.

[b][u]ACHIEVEMENTS[/u]:[/b] This straightforward list hides the difficulty behind completing it.  Any stage that has an achievement for it is one of the harder levels in the game, though special mention must go to Blobnet & Blobdance for their reliance on random enemy movements, & Force Field for the horrible visual layout.  Don't be ashamed to get maps for stages to at least see what's up ahead, & cross your fingers on some stages to eventually clear all levels & pop that final achievement.

[b][u]FINAL[/u]:[/b] Chip's Challenge is a puzzle game that sadly loses it's identity as a puzzle game the further it progresses.  Though the core gameplay loop is fun & provides plenty of opportunity for challenge, the latter stages show how frustrating, & in some cases unfair, this game truly can be.  Though due to it's nature of being free & the enjoyment & challenge some of the puzzles can give, it's easily worth a shot.

Chip's Challenge is a stalwart classic of early DOS/Windows gaming, and the rerelease is much improved, with many of the errors fixed, fancier graphics more resembling the original Lynx version, and of course the long-awaited sequel.

But the thing is that it's also very much an artifact of its time. While the game starts off reasonably friendly you will sooner than later come upon the tropes of design of the early 90s: strict trial and error puzzle solving, tedious sokoban levels where the threat of failure is more from zoning out or holding a movement key too long than actual errors in your solution, and of course, pure RNG movement. Most of the levels after 100 or so are chores, at best. If you've still got a hankering to play CC like you remember, at least do yourself a favor and play the levels in Lexy's Labyrinth, a compatible remake with new levels and graphics and most importantly, a rewind function.

My personal recommendation, though, would be to skip the Pain of Level 134 entirely and play the much more consistent Chip's Challenge 2, or one of the many excellent community level packs, instead.

I have very fond memories of playing this game many years ago on an old computer still running Windows 98, so I was quite happy when it was released on Steam some 25 years later, and I had a great time playing through these levels from my childhood again. However, this enjoyment was almost purely nostalgia, as puzzle game design has come a long way from the days of Windows 98. While there are a bunch of really fun, creative puzzle levels in this game, there are also many that are either extremely long and tedious, where a single mistake can force you to repeat 10 or more minutes of work, or heavily based on trial-and-error, with hidden hazards, secret traps, and dead ends that are unavoidable unless you know they're there. This is obviously not great puzzle design and can be pretty frustrating at times. The game does let you skip levels whenever you wish though, so you're always free to skip a level if you really don't want to complete it.

Even from a pure nostalgia perspective, this game isn't perfect either. The UI doesn't match the UI from the original game, the game defaults to a new set of textures (although you can select the old textures thankfully), and the game behaviour doesn't quite match the original (the sound for collecting a chip and a key are the same sound, some visuals/sounds update or play at the wrong time occasionally, and teleporters don't always seem to function quite like they're supposed to). The audio settings don't seem to apply properly when opening the game either, and I often get blasted by extremely loud game music when I open the game, although opening the settings and closing them again seems to apply the settings properly.

However, despite the outdated puzzle design and the imperfect replication of the original game, it's free, so I still recommend giving it a try, especially if you have fond memories of the original game like me or if you're interested in playing a piece of video game history.

[b]TL;DR[/b] This is a classic puzzle game from an era of computing that has come and gone. While it is a great blast from the past and has some decent puzzles, there's also lots of puzzles that are tedious or rely far to heavily on trial-and-error and doesn't quite replicate everything from the original game properly. However, if you have fond memories of this game or want to play a piece of video game history, then I'd recommend trying it out.
